blocks.text: And the painted partridge, and the speckled Numidian hens.
If we had birds of Libya and of Phasis, you would receive them: but as it is, receive birds of the farmyard.

Yet of these Varro says: These were the latest to come from the kitchen into the gluttons' dining-room, owing to the fastidiousness of men. And Pliny: They are the most recent of foreign birds to be admitted to the table, on account of their unpleasant smell. So rarity alone seems to have raised their price. Varro teaches us this in these words: They sell at a high price because of their scarcity. [col. 134] Likewise Petronius:
The bird sought from Phasian Colchis and the African fowl please the palate because they are not easy to get. — — ^{(1)}

So much for the various interpretations of the word ברבורים barburim. Of these, although the third and fourth may be tolerated, the first pleases me most. I mean that most ancient one, according to which ברבורים אבוסים are all the choicest fattened fowl. For, to say nothing of the agreement of the Elders with the Talmudists in asserting it, analogy requires it. Just as from חרר charar, to burn, comes חרחור charchur, extreme burning, Deut. XXVIII, 22., so from ברר barar, to choose, comes ברבור barbur, a most choice thing; the first radical is doubled so that the meaning is intensified. This is customary in these languages. Thus, since קלל means to be light or to be worthless, קלקל is a most worthless, most light, most despised thing. And the Jews, murmuring, call the manna so in contempt, Numer. XXXI, 5. And from צלל, to overshadow, comes צלצל, a denser shadow. And from רבב, to make great, come רברבים [II, 707], the magnates, who stand out most among the people. And from כידור, spark, comes כרכר, the Carchedonian stone, a gem that sparkles exceedingly. Publilius Syrus in Petronius Arbiter:
Why do you desire Carchedonian stony fires, except that they may sparkle? — — —

And from דקק, to make thin, comes דקדוק, a subtle disquisition. Hence Grammar is so called by the Hebrews, because it is a subtle and precise examination of speech. Moreover, this explanation yields a most fitting sense. Solomon's provisions for each day were thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and a hundred sheep, besides harts, roebucks, and bubali, and all the choicest fattened fowl, that is, those animals which were selected from among the rest to be fattened in a special way and set on the royal table. The ancients understood this chiefly of birds, both because small birds hold the first place in the delicacy market, and in order to distinguish them from those already mentioned, namely oxen, sheep, harts, roebucks and bubali. Yet this is not necessary, since the very method of fattening sufficiently distinguishes these from the rest; from it they are called אבוסים abusim, that is, fattened at the stall, not, like the others, in the pastures. For אבוס ebus is a stall (manger), Iob. XXXIX, 12. Prov. XIV, 14. and Es. I, 3. Hence אבס abas means to fatten livestock, not in any way whatever, but tied at the stall, and indeed with food put and thrust into the mouth, if we believe the Talmudists. Aquila renders it φατνιάζεσθαι [phatniazesthai], and Theodotion φατνεύεσθαι [phatneuesthai]. But there was no need to coin new words, since σιτεύειν [siteuein] means this. For σιτευτὰ [siteuta] is said of animals that are fattened in confinement. Hence Plutarch, Sympos. 4, Question 1: Ὅσα δὲ σιτεύουσι καθείρξαντες [hosa de siteuousi katheirxantes], Whatever they fatten shut up. So the same Theodotion renders שור אבוס as βοῦν σιτευτὸν [boun siteuton], quite rightly. And in Luc. XV, 23. the prodigal's father orders τὸν μόσχον τὸν σιτευτὸν [ton moschon ton siteuton] to be killed, that is, השור האבוס: out of many oxen or calves, the one that had been fattened in this way. For the article placed before it is not idle. And Matth. XXII, 4. τὰ σιτιστὰ τεθυμένα [ta sitista tethymena], that is, האבוסות. Accordingly, one of the Greeks renders ברבורים אבוסים as ἐκλεκτῶν σιτευτά [eklektōn siteuta]. Somewhat parallel to the passage under discussion is another, Nehem. V, 18., in which for Nehemiah's daily food are prepared one ox, six choice sheep, and birds. Choice in Hebrew is בררות, which with the first letter doubled could have been called ברברות. For בררות and ברברות are the same, except that in ברברות the meaning is more intense because of the doubled letter. So if ברורות means choice, ברברות would mean most choice ^{(2)}.
